Torsk.description: Atlantic cod is Norway's most important food fish, found along the entire coast. It is most active when pressure is falling, which triggers feeding behavior in schools. Best fishing occurs in cold water between 4 and 8 °C, particularly in deep water during winter.
Torsk.season: Found along the entire coast year-round. Bites best January–March during the spawning migration when cod congregate on shallow banks.
Torsk.teknikktips: Vary the retrieval speed with frequent pauses – imitates an injured prey and triggers the bite reflex.
Torsk.fargetips: Bottom feeding: yellow/red · Herring feeding: silver/bright
Torsk.fraLandTips: Fish during dusk hours when cod move into shallower water. Find drop-offs or deep channels within 50–100 m reach. Use lures under 30 g with a large surface area to keep the rig above kelp forests during retrieval.
Torsk.fraBåtTips: Use a pirk of at least 250 g for vertical fishing and precise bottom contact. Continuously adjust weight relative to current and drift. Use sonar to locate banks, tops and ledges – cod usually stay right down at the substrate.

Kveite.description: Halibut is Norway's largest flatfish and can exceed 300 kg. It is primarily a deep-water fish that follows tidal movements to hunt other fish. Large and powerful – halibut requires patience and the right equipment.
Kveite.season: Available year-round, but bites best August–September. Activity increases with the summer warming of coastal waters.
Kveite.teknikktips: Wait 2–3 seconds after the strike – halibut tastes the bait before swallowing it. Circle hook size 8/0 recommended.
Kveite.fraLandTips: Shore fishing requires extremely robust gear. Use large hooks (7/0+) and secure the bait with bait elastic so whole herring or mackerel fillet doesn't fall off during powerful casts. Find channels with strong current or fjord outlets. Calibrate the drag carefully – too loose and the fish gets stuck in rock piles, too tight and the line snaps.
Kveite.fraBåtTips: Use sonar to locate concentrations of baitfish – halibut follows its prey. Use large rubber jigs or whole coalfish as bait. Chase the fish during explosive runs rather than braking – it significantly reduces the risk of line breaks.

Sei.description: Coalfish is a fast, schooling fish that actively hunts in the water column. It thrives in moderate current and is particularly active at dusk when light is low. Coalfish is found along the entire Norwegian coast and is a popular sport fish.
Sei.season: Found along the coast year-round with two peak biting periods: May (spring inflow) and October (autumn inflow). Least active midsummer and midwinter.
Sei.teknikktips: Reel in as fast as possible – speed triggers the hunting instinct and gives the fish no time to inspect the bait critically.
Sei.fargetips: Rubber sandeel: red, white and glow-in-dark green are classic choices
Sei.fraLandTips: Schools of small coalfish patrol along steep rock faces and breakwaters during the middle of the day. Use reels with a high gear ratio and rods that can handle powerful runs. Reel fast – coalfish are visual hunters that respond to speed, not the bait's appearance.
Sei.fraBåtTips: Jigging and trolling are the dominant methods. Use sonar to distinguish between dense schools of small coalfish and the more scattered echoes of large coalfish, which tend to be deeper. Use a robust rod and thick line – full jigging gear under retrieval creates enormous strain.

Hyse.description: Haddock is closely related to cod, but slimmer with a characteristic dark shoulder patch. It is most active during falling air pressure and lives near the bottom on sand and shell sand. Haddock puts up a good fight on light tackle.
Hyse.season: Available year-round. Bites best April–May and is consistently good through autumn.
sluk: Rigs with beads and spinner blades
Hyse.teknikktips: Haddock is curious about colors and lights – use a rig with beads and spinner blades to increase catch rates.
Hyse.fargetips: Attractors: pink, white and yellow are most effective · Glow details increase catch
Hyse.fraLandTips: Haddock tastes the bait before swallowing – use a sensitive rod tip to register the faint bites at 40–50 m depth. Fish on sand and shell sand bottoms. Haddock is often bycatch when bottom fishing, but responds well to attractors like beads and spinner blades.
Hyse.fraBåtTips: Use a light sea fishing rod with a soft tip to pick up the gentle bites. Present shrimp or blue mussel just above the bottom. Haddock concentrates in specific soft-bottom areas – use a chartplotter to mark productive spots.

Lange.description: Ling is an elongated codfish that lives on deep, hard bottoms. It prefers calm water with little current and is particularly active during rising tide. Ling's long body and gentle bite require a certain technique.
Lange.season: Available year-round in deep water. Bites best May–June. Its depth preference makes it little affected by seasonal surface temperature fluctuations.
Lange.teknikktips: Keep the bait 2–5 meters above the bottom and in motion – ling hunts actively, unlike the stationary cusk.
Lange.fraLandTips: Shore fishing is nearly impossible due to depth preference of 100–1000 m. Exceptions exist in some western fjords where the mountainside drops vertically to deep water just a few meters from shore. Requires weights of 150–200 g and extremely strong tackle. Fish easily get stuck in rock piles during ascent.
Lange.fraBåtTips: Seek deep ledges and steep slopes (400–600 m) with chartplotter and sonar. Use a reel with large line capacity for braided line and lead weights over 500 g to keep the bait vertical. The boat's ability to hold position in current is crucial for success.

Brosme.description: Cusk is a deep-water fish with a long dorsal fin and a powerful barbel under the chin. It inhabits rocky bottoms and coral reefs in deep water. Cusk is a tough fighter and tastes excellent smoked or salted.
Brosme.season: Available year-round. Bites best May–June. Lives so deep that surface seasonal fluctuations have little effect on willingness to bite.
Brosme.teknikktips: Let the bait rest right down on the bottom – cusk barely moves vertically and is very stationary.
Brosme.fraLandTips: Shore fishing is practically impossible – cusk prefers rocky and hard bottom at 100–1000 m depth. Fishing from shore is only feasible where steep fjord walls provide access to deep water directly from the shoreline.
Brosme.fraBåtTips: Find rocky bottom and steep deep ledges with sonar. Let the bait (fresh mackerel or herring) rest completely on the bottom – cusk is stationary and won't hunt upward. Use heavy weights and glow details to attract attention in the darkness of deep water.

Uer.description: Ocean perch is a long-lived red fish that can live over 100 years. It is nocturnal and thrives in stable weather with little movement in the water masses. Large ocean perch inhabit deep water in fjords and along the outer coast.
Uer.season: Available year-round. Bites best June–July. Ocean perch is extremely long-lived (100+ years) and the population is vulnerable – consider releasing large individuals.
Uer.teknikktips: Ocean perch congregates in dense schools many meters above the bottom – use long rigs (up to 20 m) to search through the entire water column.
Uer.fraLandTips: Shore fishing is practically impossible – ocean perch lives at 100–1000 m depth and is not accessible from land. Focus on other species from the pier.
Uer.fraBåtTips: Use rigs with many hooks baited with fish pieces, combined with glow slugs to attract fish in the darkness. NOTE: ocean perch does not survive the pressure change during ascent (barotrauma) – this is purely harvest fishing where catch-and-release is not possible.

Steinbit.description: Atlantic wolffish has a large, rounded head with powerful teeth that can crush shells and crabs. It inhabits rocky bottoms in cold water and is active year-round. Wolffish is fearless and bites well in stable weather.
Steinbit.season: Available year-round along the Norwegian coast. Bites best July–August, but is active even in winter in cold water.
sluk: Bottom rig with paternoster and slider
Steinbit.teknikktips: Spinner blades and heavy beads can irritate wolffish into striking – it is territorial and aggressive.
Steinbit.fraLandTips: Bottom fishing with crushed blue mussel or shrimp where deep channels run close to shore. Be prepared that wolffish wedge themselves under rocks when hooked – use solid tackle. Watch out for the teeth when unhooking.
Steinbit.fraBåtTips: Repeatedly thump a heavy weight against the bottom to create sound and vibrations – this irritates the territorial wolffish into striking. Use a stiff rod and a reel with good drag. Kelp forest edges and shell sand banks near current-rich channels are ideal positions.

Makrell.description: Mackerel is a fast, schooling fish that enters Norwegian coastal waters during summer when the water is warm. It bites best in light to moderate breeze that ripples the surface. Mackerel is known for its intense fights and is excellent food.
Makrell.season: Seasonal fish: arrives along the Norwegian coast May–June and leaves in September–October. Absent in winter. Peak biting period is July–August.
Makrell.teknikktips: Keep the lure just below the surface with small twitches of the rod – significantly increases willingness to bite.
Makrell.fraLandTips: Find times when mackerel is pushed toward shore by coalfish or cod. Rising tide often brings the schools closer in. Use light casting lures or rigs and reel fast – mackerel responds to speed and movement.
Makrell.fraBåtTips: Trolling at 2–3 knots with lures or wobblers is the dominant method. Cover large sea areas to locate the schools. When you find them, mark the position and fish intensively – mackerel can disappear as quickly as it arrived.

Rødspette.description: Plaice is a colorful flatfish with characteristic orange spots on the upper side. It is found on sandy bottoms in shallow coastal waters and is particularly active during rising tide. Plaice is a delicacy and gives good sport on light tackle.
Rødspette.season: Available in coastal waters year-round. Bites best May–June. Activity decreases somewhat in winter in cold water.
sluk: Beads and spinner blades as attractors
Rødspette.teknikktips: Tap the weight lightly against the bottom to stir up sediments – attracts plaice's curiosity.
Rødspette.fargetips: Attractors: white, pearl, yellow and red are most effective
Rødspette.fraLandTips: Cast out and let the bait rest on sandy bottom, interrupted by short retrieves that stir up sediments. Use visual attractors (white/red beads and spinner blades) to lure the fish to the bait. Fish at 5–40 m depth.
Rødspette.fraBåtTips: Drift over large sand flats to find concentrations of fish. Use a light sea fishing rod (7–8 ft) with soft tip. A slider rig with long leaders along the bottom is effective – control the drift speed carefully, too fast and the bait lifts off the bottom.

Lomre.description: Witch flounder is the smallest of the Norwegian flatfish and lives on sandy bottoms in calm, shallow waters. It is undemanding to fish for, but requires fine bait close to the bottom. Good eating despite its modest size.
Lomre.season: Available year-round. Bites best May–June. Witch flounder is stationary and little affected by temperature fluctuations – seasonal variation is modest.
Lomre.teknikktips: Let the bait rest completely still – witch flounder sucks in prey from the bottom and doesn't respond to movement.
Lomre.fraLandTips: Fish on stony sandy bottom at 20–100 m depth. Witch flounder has a very small mouth – use the smallest hooks (size 4–8) and cut bait (shrimp/blue mussel) into tiny pieces. Let the bait rest completely still.
Lomre.fraBåtTips: Drift slowly over sand flats using light tackle with a soft rod tip. Witch flounder is often bycatch – mark positions where you find it, as it tends to stay in the same area. The technique is similar to plaice fishing, but with finer gear.

Sandflyndre.description: Dab resembles witch flounder but is slightly more elongated and prefers somewhat deeper sandy bottoms. It is prey for halibut and cod, but can also be caught on light line with worm. Dab has good flavor from Norwegian coastal waters.
Sandflyndre.season: Available year-round. Bites best May–June. Little seasonal variation – remains stable on sandy bottom throughout the year.
Sandflyndre.teknikktips: Lift the bait slowly and set it back down at regular intervals – dab likes bait in motion.
Sandflyndre.fraLandTips: Fish on muddy and sandy bottom at 10–150 m depth. Lift the bait slowly and set it back down at regular intervals. Dab is widespread and often bycatch, but concentrates in soft-bottom areas outside river mouths.
Sandflyndre.fraBåtTips: Drift over large sand flats with light tackle. Trailing technique where the bait is dragged along the bottom is effective. Dab is one of the most accessible species from a boat and provides good sport on light sea fishing gear.

Sild.description: Herring migrate in large schools along the Norwegian coast and are a keystone species in the marine ecosystem. Most active in cool to temperate water, often concentrating in large schools around full moon and new moon. Herring is a classic Norwegian food fish.
Sild.season: Two peaks: March (spawning along the coast) and November (autumn herring season). Found along the coast year-round, but easiest to catch during school concentrations.
Sild.teknikktips: Use a rig with many small hooks and fine line – the flies should imitate plankton and small fish in the school.
Sild.fraLandTips: Fish with herring rigs from pier or breakwater at night when the schools move in toward shore. Use fine line and many small hooks. Herring bites easiest in the dark – light from the pier can attract plankton and thereby the herring.
Sild.fraBåtTips: Fish deeper than mackerel with herring rigs. NOTE: herring have a very soft mouth – use smooth and gentle retrieval to avoid the hook tearing out. Sonar is indispensable for finding schools in the dark water column.

Laks.description: Salmon is a legendary sport fish that returns to the river where it hatched. In saltwater, salmon bites best at dusk during falling air pressure. It is a powerful fighter that requires good gear and patience from the angler.
Laks.season: Marine phase May–August. From August the salmon moves toward rivers for spawning. Be aware of protection zones at river mouths.
Laks.teknikktips: Choose lure color based on the river's color tone – the match between the lure and the water color is crucial.
Laks.fargetips: Clear river: silver/blue · Cognac-colored: gold/copper · Flood water: orange/red
Laks.fraLandTips: In river: find good positions behind rocks, in current edges and in deep pools. Choose lure color based on the river's color tone. Be aware of protection zones around river mouths where fishing may be prohibited to protect the spawning stock.
Laks.fraBåtTips: Trolling along the shore and in fjords. Use a downrigger to precisely control the bait depth – salmon migrates in specific water layers depending on salinity and temperature. Navigate actively around protection zones at river mouths.

Sjøørret.description: Sea trout is the sea-migrating form of brown trout and is found along the coast in saltwater for parts of the year. It is very temperature-sensitive and bites best in low light during falling pressure. Sea trout is known for wild leaps and spectacular fights on light tackle.
Sjøørret.season: In the sea April–September with peaks in May–June and again in September. Check local protection rules – in many places protected from October 1.
Sjøørret.teknikktips: Sink pause is critical – let the lure sink 2–3 seconds at regular intervals. Most strikes come at the change of direction.
Sjøørret.fargetips: 7–17 °C: holographic silver/black or silver/blue · Cold water: pink, orange or white/fluorescent
Sjøørret.fraLandTips: Find leopard bottom – a mosaic of sand, rock and seaweed belts. Sea trout is extremely shy in clear water; long casts and careful approach are crucial. Two hours before and after high tide is the best time. Fish over large areas with light lures.
Sjøørret.fraBåtTips: Trolling along the shore and in fjords with a downrigger for precise depth control. Keep a good distance from shore and cast toward the beach. Navigate around protection zones at river mouths – sea trout congregates here before the spawning migration.

Sjørøye.description: Sea-run Arctic char is the northernmost of the anadromous salmonids and thrives in cold arctic water. It migrates between fresh and saltwater and is known for its intense colors during spawning season. Arctic char is a delicacy with firm, pink flesh.
Sjørøye.season: Marine phase June–August. Returns to freshwater for spawning in autumn. Limited to fjord systems in Northern Norway and Svalbard.
Sjørøye.teknikktips: Similar technique to sea trout – sink pause with 2–3 second pauses. Mostly linked to fjord systems in Northern Norway.
Sjørøye.fargetips: Colorful and contrasting varieties are generally most effective
Sjørøye.fraLandTips: Shore fishing is the most effective method – Arctic char stays very close to shore and river mouths. Use a wide selection of flies and small lures, as char can be very selective. Be aware that pink salmon can outcompete Arctic char in the marine phase in some river systems.
Sjørøye.fraBåtTips: Rarely necessary as Arctic char stays coastal, but light coastal fishing from a rowboat or kayak along river mouths and shallow fjord beaches can give good results. Use the same technique as for sea trout.

Ørret.description: Brown trout is one of Norway's most sought-after sport fish and is found in rivers and lakes across the country. It is most active during falling air pressure and bites well in the ideal temperature window of 8–14 °C. Trout is a tactical and demanding fish.
Ørret.season: Active April–October with peaks in May–June and September. Inactive under ice in winter. Protection regulations vary greatly – always check local rules.
Ørret.teknikktips: Aura Flake with disco-ball surface is effective under almost all light conditions. Match fly type to the season's insect hatch.
Ørret.fargetips: Clear water/sun: natural colors and silver · Murky/overcast: gold, copper and fluorescent
Ørret.fraLandTips: Line control is crucial in rivers – the lure or fly must drift naturally without the line tightening. Fish upstream so you don't alert the fish. In low summer rivers, trout is extra shy; wade carefully and keep low.
Ørret.fraBåtTips: From canoe or river boat: drift slowly downstream and cast toward the shore or toward deep channels. This gives access to spots with dense vegetation along the bank that are impossible to reach from shore. In lakes, a boat is necessary to reach the deep trout in summer.

Røye.description: Arctic char is a cold-water species that thrives best in deep, clear lakes. It bites well during falling pressure in cool water and is particularly active in autumn during spawning season. Arctic char is Norway's most beautiful freshwater fish with its characteristic colors.
Røye.season: Bites best September–February in cold water. In summer, char retreats to deep, cold layers and is then little accessible from shore.
Røye.teknikktips: Copper colors are superior for Arctic char, especially at low light and in the evening.
Røye.fargetips: Evening/low light: copper and red · Daylight: natural trout colors
Røye.fraLandTips: Accessible from shore in spring and autumn when char moves up to shallower areas. In summer it retreats to the deepest, coldest water layers and is then inaccessible from shore. Use insect imitations and copper colors at low light.
Røye.fraBåtTips: Sonar and deep bait are necessary in summer to reach char in the deep water layers. Char appears in large schools – when you find the schools, fishing can be very effective. Be aware of overpopulation of char in many lakes, which results in small stunted fish.

Abbor.description: Perch is one of the most common freshwater fish in Norway and is recognizable by the vertical stripes along its body. It is a warm-water fish and bites best in summer at dusk. Perch often congregates around vegetation and structures near shore.
Abbor.season: Active May–September with peak June–August. Nearly inactive in winter in cold water – the biting window is strongly temperature-dependent.
Abbor.teknikktips: Spinners send out strong pressure waves – ideal for quickly locating active fish in the school.
Abbor.fargetips: Imitating prey: green, brown, orange · Aggression: yellow and red
Abbor.fraLandTips: Focus on structures like piers, sunken trees and the edge of reed belts. The largest perch often hold deeper and more sheltered than small perch – in lakes with smelt, large fish can go down to 20+ m and are hard to reach from shore.
Abbor.fraBåtTips: Spot shooting with jigs or dropshot rig directly on sonar echoes is very effective. Perch appears in schools – locate a school and fish intensively in the spot. In lakes with much roach, perch rarely go deeper than 7 m.

Gjedde.description: Pike is the apex predator in Norwegian lakes and rivers with its characteristic duck bill and powerful body. It is an ambush predator that likes low light and waits quietly for prey. Large pike can weigh over 10 kg and are one of the most exciting sport fish in freshwater.
Gjedde.season: Two peak biting periods: April–May (right after spawning) and September–October. Semi-inactive midsummer in warm water.
Gjedde.teknikktips: Always use a wire leader – pike teeth cut regular line immediately.
Gjedde.fargetips: Murky water: strong colors (Fire Tiger) · Clear water: natural colors (perch/pike pattern)
Gjedde.fraLandTips: Use weedless lures (hooks protected against snagging) to fish inside the densest reed belts and under water lilies – where pike hides. Cast along the vegetation edge and let the bait sink. Always use a wire leader.
Gjedde.fraBåtTips: Fish along the vegetation edge from outside in, or troll over open water for large pike that may follow vendace/smelt schools pelagically. NOTE safety: handling large pike with hundreds of razor-sharp teeth requires sturdy pliers and unhooking equipment.

Harr.description: Grayling is known for its impressive sail-like dorsal fin and is found in clear, fast-flowing rivers with good water quality. It is a delicate fly fish that rises to the surface to take insects. Grayling is demanding to trick and rewards you with spectacular leaps.
Harr.season: Best season May–June during the intensive insect hatch. Active through summer, but more selective after June – evening hours are then most important.
Harr.teknikktips: Red Tag with red tag detail is grayling fly #1 – the red detail acts as a powerful visual trigger.
Harr.fargetips: Early season: bright/silver spinner · Autumn: subtle and natural colors
Harr.fraLandTips: Wading is standard – wade out to shallow areas to reach the current edges where grayling holds at 1–4 m depth. Use small flies and hooks (grayling has a small mouth). Wade carefully – grayling is very sensitive to vibrations in the water.
Harr.fraBåtTips: From canoe or river boat: drift slowly downstream while casting toward shore or toward deep channels in the middle of the river. Gives access to spots along the bank with dense vegetation that are impossible to reach from shore. Use a light fly rod or ultralight spinning gear.
